plan.geometry_notes: World scale: guide sphere radius R = 2 units centered at origin. The silhouette is a single circle of radius 2 in the screen plane (XY), stroked in grey #888888, linewidth ~2px — do NOT render a transparent filled sphere that would obscure this outline. Equatorial ellipse: semi-major axis = 2 (horizontal, along X), semi-minor axis ≈ 0.6 (vertical compression to suggest tilt), color #bbbbbb, thin stroke. Vertical dashed polar axis from (0, -2.4, 0) to (0, 2.4, 0), grey #999999. Horizontal dashed equatorial axis from (-2.4, 0, 0) to (2.4, 0, 0), grey #999999. Proton at origin: dark blue #1a3a8f disc radius 0.18 with white '+' text. Electron at spherical position theta ≈ 50° from +Y (upward), phi ≈ 40° to the right of vertical — placing it clearly in the upper-right quadrant of the circle; pale blue #6fb3d8, radius 0.12. Partial meridian arc: a blue #5599cc arc from the top of the silhouette circle (0, 2, 0) curving down to the electron position — this is NOT a full ellipse, just the portion from top to electron. Radial line r: black, from origin to electron; label 'r' in bold black font size ~16px placed at the midpoint offset 0.2 units above (perpendicular to the line, toward upper-left). Force arrow F: red #cc2222, tail at electron, pointing toward proton; length = 3/r² capped at 2.0; label 'F' in bold red font size ~16px placed beside the arrow offset 0.25 units to the right. Projection guides: faint blue #88bbdd dashed lines — one vertical from electron down to equatorial plane, one horizontal from that foot to the X-axis. Physics: |F| = ke²/r² with k = 8.99×10⁹ N·m²/C², e = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C.
plan.notes: Three.js: Draw the silhouette circle as a LineLoop (or thick-stroked ring) in the XY plane — do NOT add a transparent SphereGeometry that would wash out the outline. The equatorial ellipse is a separate LineLoop scaled in Y to ~0.3× the circle radius to suggest a tilted plane. The partial meridian arc is a THREE.EllipseCurve or catmull-rom from (0,2,0) to the electron's position, drawn as a simple line — not a full ellipse. All dashed lines use LineDashedMaterial with computeLineDistances(). The F arrow uses ArrowHelper or a custom cone+cylinder. Labels 'r' and 'F' use CSS2DRenderer or sprite text at font size 16px+, positioned with explicit offsets to avoid overlapping the lines they annotate. On slider change, recompute electron position along its fixed angular direction at the new radius, update the arc endpoint, the r-line endpoint, and the F-arrow length and position. The entire scene is essentially a 2D schematic (axis_screen_angles: null) with 3D depth cues provided by the equatorial ellipse and projection guides.

authoredPrompt: This figure is a schematic three-dimensional depiction of a hydrogen atom drawn as one large sphere. The sphere is rendered as a grey outline circle with a paler grey ellipse across its middle standing for an equatorial plane, which gives the drawing depth. At the center sits a small dark blue disc bearing a plus sign, representing the proton. A second, much smaller pale blue sphere representing the electron is placed on the upper right of the spherical surface, and a thin blue arc curves down to it from the top of the sphere. A straight black line labeled r joins the central charge to the electron, and a thick red arrow labeled F lies along that same line, pointing from the electron back toward the nucleus. A vertical dashed line through the center, a horizontal dashed line across the equatorial ellipse, and faint blue dashed guides dropping from the electron to that ellipse fix the electron's position in three dimensions. Drawing the force antiparallel to r conveys at a glance that the interaction is attractive and directed along the line joining the two particles. The sketch sets up a Coulomb's law calculation of the force on the ground-state electron at its most probable distance from the proton.
authoredInteractions:
- Drag for moving the electron on the spherical guide: the learner repositions the electron, the r segment and F arrow rotate so F always points back toward the proton, making the attractive central-force direction explicit.
- Slider for electron-proton separation: the learner changes r, the electron moves along the radius and the force arrow length rescales by inverse-square strength, showing how Coulomb force direction stays radial while magnitude depends on distance.
authoredContext:
The Force on the Electron in Hydrogen A hydrogen atom consists of a single proton and a single electron. The proton has a charge of +e and the electron has −e. In the “ground state” of the atom, the electron orbits the proton at most probable distance of 5.29×10−11m (the figure). Calculate the electric force on the electron due to the proton.

A schematic depiction of a hydrogen atom, showing the force on the electron. This depiction is only to enable us to calculate the force; the hydrogen atom does not really look like this. Recall another section.

A positive charge is shown at the center of a sphere of radius r. An electron is depicted as a particle on the sphere. The force on the electron is along the radius, toward the nucleus.

Strategy For the purposes of this example, we are treating the electron and proton as two point particles, each with an electric charge, and we are told the distance between them; we are asked to calculate the force on the electron. We thus use Coulomb’s law.

interactionPlan.notes: Three.js: render the guide sphere as a low-opacity grey shell plus LineLoop silhouettes for the equator and one meridian; use an ArrowHelper (or cone+cylinder group) for F and a Line for r, both parented to a group oriented by the electron's spherical angles so drag updates theta/phi and the slider updates radius. Dashed lines via LineDashedMaterial with computeLineDistances(), recomputed each frame. On drag, raycast the pointer onto the sphere of radius r to set electron direction; on slider change, scale the electron position and F length. Keep the camera fixed (no orbit) so the schematic matches the source viewpoint; the drag gesture is reserved for moving the electron, not the camera.
